hydration.reasoning: EFSA adequate intake for adult men is 2.5 L/day TOTAL water, of which ~20% comes from food, so ~2.0 L from drinks for a reference man in a temperate climate. ICMR-NIN guidance for India works out to roughly 32-58 ml/kg for men (~2.7-4.8 L total at 83 kg) and Indian guidance adds +0.5-1 L for hot/humid climate and activity. Subject is 83 kg (above reference weight), trains daily at 5:30 AM (~0.5-1 L sweat loss per session), lives in Bangalore (mild-warm, not extreme heat), and eats a fibre-heavy dal/legume diet. Net: ~3 L drunk water on rest days, ~3.5-4 L on training days. Actionable: 3 x 1L bottles on rest days, 4 x 1L bottles on training days (first ~500 ml before/during the 5:30 AM session).
hydration.source_url: https://www.nutrition.org.uk/nutritional-information/hydration/ (fetched; cites EFSA AI 2.5 L/day men, 20% from food, heat/exercise adjustment, hyponatraemia warning). Also: EFSA Journal 2010;8(3):1459 https://efsa.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.2903/j.efsa.2010.1459 (paywalled) and ICMR-NIN Dietary Guidelines for Indians 2024 https://nin.res.in/dietaryguidelines/pdfjs/locale/DGI_2024.pdf
hydration.caveat: Do not force it. Spread intake across the day and keep it under ~1 L/hour; chugging several litres quickly, or drinking far beyond thirst during long exercise, risks hyponatraemia (dangerously low sodium). Pale-straw urine is the target; on heavy-sweat days add a pinch of salt/electrolytes rather than more plain water.
hydration.fibre_note: A high-fibre diet (dal/chana/rajma daily) slightly raises water need: fibre absorbs water in the gut and needs it to do its job. The same legumes also carry cooking water, so this nudges the target up ~0.25-0.5 L rather than adding a full bottle. Bonus: sipping water is a useful craving-displacement tool during this change.

supplements.name: Magnesium glycinate
supplements.why: Sleep quality and muscle recovery for a daily 5:30 AM trainer; magnesium status is commonly marginal on refined-grain-heavy diets.
supplements.form_note: Glycinate (bisglycinate) is the gentle, well-absorbed form - it rarely causes loose stools. Oxide is the cheap form on many Indian labels: poorly absorbed (~4%) and a laxative at these doses. Citrate absorbs decently but is more laxative than glycinate. KEY TRAP: '2000 mg magnesium glycinate' on Indian labels is the COMPOUND weight - only ~10-14% is elemental magnesium. Read the elemental number, not the headline number.

supplements.name: Vitamin D3 (cholecalciferol)
supplements.why: Indoor-heavy urban Indian lifestyles are strongly associated with low vitamin D; supports bone, muscle and mood - relevant during this change.
supplements.form_note: D3 (cholecalciferol) raises blood levels better and for longer than D2 (ergocalciferol) - everything listed here is D3. It is fat-soluble: take with the fattiest meal of the day (breakfast with ghee/nuts/eggs works). Softgels in oil and chewables both absorb fine; the oil-based capsule is the safest default.

supplements.name: Omega-3 fish oil
supplements.dose: 1-2 g EPA+DHA per day (not 1-2 g 'fish oil')
supplements.timing: breakfast, with fat (same meal as D3)
supplements.why: Anti-inflammatory support for daily training and cardiovascular support while recovery.
supplements.form_note: THE TRAP: 'Fish oil 1000 mg' is the oil weight, not the omega-3 dose. Many cheap Indian softgels deliver only ~300 mg EPA+DHA per 1000 mg capsule, so a '1 g' habit is actually 0.3 g - you need 3-4 caps/day to hit 1 g, which erases the price advantage. Read EPA+DHA per capsule. Form: natural triglyceride (TG) oils absorb somewhat better than ethyl-ester (EE) concentrates, especially away from fatty meals; concentrates (60%+) are usually EE unless the label says re-esterified/natural triglyceride. Taking any form with a fatty breakfast narrows the gap. Burp-prone? Enteric-coated or TG forms help.

supplements.name: NAC (N-acetyl cysteine) 600 mg
supplements.why: Glutathione precursor with evidence for airway mucus clearance - directly relevant while lungs recover.
supplements.form_note: NAC smells and tastes of sulphur (rotten egg) - that is normal chemistry, not spoilage. Plain tablets/capsules sidestep the taste; effervescent pharma versions (e.g. Mucinac) taste strongly and are best avoided unless you like the fizz. Take with water; if it niggles an empty stomach post-workout, move it to lunch.

supplements.form_note: Plain ascorbic acid is fully effective - fancy 'ester' or liposomal forms are not worth paying for at this dose. Chewables contain sugar/sweetener; take with food if it ever feels acidic on an empty stomach.

gp_signoff_note: Run the whole five-item stack past your GP once before starting - one conversation covers everything. Flag NAC specifically (it interacts with nitroglycerin and some blood-pressure medication) and agree the D3 dose off a blood test. Nothing here replaces prescribed medication.
d3_test_first: Test serum 25-OH-D before buying D3. 1000-2000 IU/day is a MAINTENANCE dose; if the test shows deficiency (<20 ng/mL), the standard Indian protocol your GP will likely use is 60,000 IU once weekly for 6-8 weeks (prescription sachets, ~Rs 30-50 each), then step down to daily maintenance. The test costs ~Rs 700-1,500 in Bangalore labs.

amla_note.what: Amla for the recovery shot is a grocery, not a supplement: Patanjali Divya Amla Churna 100 g covers about a month at ~3 g/day; fresh amla shows up in Bangalore markets and on Blinkit/BigBasket roughly Oct-Mar at ~Rs 60-120/kg (estimated) - use fresh in season, powder the rest of the year. Ginger, turmeric, lemon, honey and black pepper are ordinary kitchen shopping.
